Feature Translation: The final struggles of a batch of near-death robotics companies Context: Xu Chuan (pseudonym) still holds out hope. Even though his former employer, a Guangdong-based robotics startup, owes him six months of salary, he has not yet pursued legal action (“The boss is actually a decent person,” he reasons). Plus, he hopes that the company can recover, choosing to ignore the fact that it has consistently failed to find stable commercial footing despite several pivots. Similar stories have unfolded throughout China’s robotics industry this year. In July, Yinghe Robotics [盈合机器人], once valued at USD$500 million, completed bankruptcy procedures; two months earlier, DeepBlue Robotics, a company backed by AI unicorn DeepBlueAI, also filed for bankruptcy. The winner of last week’s Around the Horn, a longform Huxiu article by Yuqin Yi — packed with interviews and data — details why so many Chinese robotics firms are barely hanging on to life. It ties together themes from two recent ChinAI issues: China’s venture capital ecosystem’s defiance of common sense, when it comes embodied AI ( ChinAI #381 ) China’s unsustainable embodied AI sector, built on murky guanxi relationships and limited technical capabilities ( ChinAI #372 ) Key Takeaways: DeepBlue Robotics and Yinghe Robotics constitute prominent failures, but they are part of a broader trend. From the article: “ An industry insider familiar with DeepBlue recalled that the company expanded rapidly over the past few years, extending its operations from smart retail into areas like autonomous driving and robotics. Its robotics division alone spanned various categories, including cleaning, delivery, disinfection, and gardening. ‘ Basically, whatever was hot, they would do ,’ the source noted .” After the breathless reports of initial deals, what actually transpired when it came to project fulfillment? In the case of DeepBlue, nothing. For instance, in 2021, the company boasted that South Korea’s LG Group had agreed to procure tens of thousands of intelligent disinfection robots. But: “ A former DeepBlue employee stated that they were never executed on a large scale, attributing this to the products’ inability to adapt effectively to real-world operational environments .” Again, it’s not just these high-profile crashouts. Feature Translation: The 2026 VC sphere is defying common sense Context: Liu Xiaoqing is director of analysis at IT Juzi [IT桔子], one of my favorite sources on China’s venture capital ecosystem. Last week, she posted a lengthy denunciation that begins with this bold statement: ' In 2026, a year where “embodied AI” has become practically in unison with “Chinese venture capital,” there are too many things happening that run counter to common sense . Liu has seen countless founding teams that look good on paper: “ a brilliant technical lead, a former executive from a major tech firm, a supply-chain veteran, and someone well-versed in the world of capital.” In practice, whole is much less than the sum of its parts. In a piece full of zingers, this might have been my favorite one: Yet, for many teams today, the journey looks more like this: the first time you meet happens at a dinner arranged by a financial advisor, the second time you meet takes place at the negotiating table for a term sheet, and the third you meet is the signing ceremony. People with completely different backgrounds, splitting equity 40/30/30, suddenly find themselves “running a company together” from day one. That’s not called a partnership; that’s called assembling a party for a video game quest. 3) Startups look too much like big tech giants from day one. content: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI General, often expert, and sometimes jagged Ethan Mollick Nov 09, 2026 1,515 255 181 Share Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,409 236 144 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. Humans have been working on management for a very long time without fully figuring it out. It seemed like the kind of thing that would need to be designed by people, at least for a while. It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do. Which brings us to dots and Muse. content: Commitment issues (app edition) - by Ben Tossell Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in Commitment issues (app edition) It’s not me, it’s you Ben Tossell Nov 24, 2026 54 1 1 Share Last week, a mathematician spent six weeks with Claude and proved the Riemann hypothesis. A maths problem nobody had cracked since 1859. Then there’s me. I built a clock. P.s. The full interactive version of this post is here . Something in my tiny pea brain stops me working out What time is 10am PT in UK? without using super intelligence. I’m not proud of my chat history. It’s as bad as my calculator history. 200+65 is 265 btw. My clock lives in my menu bar. Type a time and a city, or drag it, and every city changes. presets for demo only It handles daylight savings too. Because of course the UK and US change their clocks on different weekends. You may be thinking ‘There’s a million clock apps that do this for free’. And you’re absolutely right. But I’ve got commitment issues. I’m always window shopping. Lots of apps are good enough but it feels like the grass is always greener. A lot of great tools come down to a few small features I really like. But they’re not making it for me. They’re making it for everyone. They need more users, so they add more features, and they put the price up. Or they’re free and get forgotten. It’s not me, it’s you. And I’m no better with AI models. Right now I’m using Gemini 4 Neon after turning my back on Google. A new model comes around and I pack my bags and move in. I obviously need the best to answer my very hard questions. The trouble with juggling multiple models at once is keeping track of them. Who am I neglecting? Who’s about to cut me off? Other apps I tried had more than I needed, so I made a stripped down version with just the things I care about. sliding usage is just used to show the menu icon syncing Screenshots are another one. I take a lot of full-page screenshots. Things I’ve built, to check them, or sites I like the look of, to ‘borrow’ from. So now I have an extension that does that. Browsers are a different beast. They’re a marriage. We spend a lot of time in them. So this relationship has been one of my biggest headaches. I’m sure I could build my own but it feels like a lot of work. I loved Arc, like many others. Then they got bought and ditched it. So I went back to Chrome. Then the people behind Arc came out with Dia, so I went crawling back to my ex, who’d had some work done. It was kinda the same but not quite. Then I dated someone literally named after both of my exes, Arc and Dia - Ardia. No red flags there. Then it got slow. So I stopped looking and just taught Chrome all my ex’s best moves: A way to ‘peek’ links - which shows you a mini window of the page you click Click to open a page in split view Vertical tabs (Chrome added this anyway) Ad blocking, no cookie banners And my biggest need - the tab switcher. I built my own extension + mac app that does all of that. Plus I can add in some extra niceties like defaultin

content: Productiv-icky - by Ben Tossell - Ben's Bites Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in Productiv-icky Digging holes on the beach Ben Tossell Nov 17, 2026 79 4 2 Share productiv-icky (adj.) - the feeling of doing work you didn’t mean to do We have a problem. full interactive post is here We agree this is insane, right? Someone I don’t know sends me emails that I’m expected to reply to. I don’t know them. I don’t work for them. So I ignore them (well actually I send them to email jail). Nuh-uh, that’s not my work, buddy. But it’s different if it’s my super-intelligent, helpful agent friend… Yeses are easy. They’re quick. But every yes has a yes-tax. The hidden extra work you didn’t think of. The long tail of regret where you question why you ever said yes. Say I did reply to those emails, they’d send me stuff to read to show how great they are at their job and how much better I’d be. Then we’d organise a call (which would derail whichever day that call was on). Then we’d have follow-up items. Then a string of other crap I couldn’t care less about. I know what’s going to happen. I can smell it, it stinks. I’ve said yes and paid the tax many times before. Now I pay $200/mo for a super-intelligent, over-eager, needy little nerd to ping me incessantly about taking things off my plate. I feel bad for him. He wants to work. He’s gagging for it. Just. One. More. Task. Master. Plus, my little nerd has a gambling problem. Or rather, he feeds mine. Remember years ago sending tons of Slack messages to get the most out of your $20/mo plan? Nor me. Why? Because it’s dumb. But now we feel like we should use all our tokens before they run out. Why? Because everyone else is. We started measuring shovels instead of the hole. Someone’s needy little nerd booked their dentist, replied to their mum and launched a business whilst they were asleep. They’ve got an org chart. For nerds. With a Chief of Staff. You feel behind. Like way behind. So you grab a shovel and start digging. A little hole over there to triage your inbox, one here to draft your tweets, one to check on those. Then you spend your day checking the holes are being dug right. Before long, you’re surrounded by holes and a mountain of dirt you gotta do something with. Now as a man, holes are hardwired into my DNA. A few beers, a beach and a shovel, I’m digging a hole. I’d take pride in it. I’d make the best one, impressively round, deep enough to see sea water seep through the bottom. But I’d only dig one. There’s a whole beach but I chose this spot. Next time the needy little nerd pings you: do you really want another hole? Also, don’t dig big holes on the beach. They collapse.
